lessons.title: Planning and preparing for small stock classification
lessons.html:
Why lamb, mutton and goat carcasses are classified

Sheep and goat carcasses slaughtered at South African abattoirs are classified so that farmers, abattoirs, butchers and consumers can trust what they are buying. Classification falls under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 and its regulations. A Karoo farmer sending a load of Dorper lambs to the abattoir is paid per kilogram according to class, so a wrong class can cost the farmer or the buyer real money.

Red meat carcasses, including small stock, are classified mainly on age, fatness, conformation (shape and muscling) and damage. The age class and fat code together make the class mark that consumers see on the meat, for example A2.

Planning the shift

  • Check the slaughter list: number of animals, producers, and whether lambs, sheep or goats are coming through.
  • Confirm your registration as a classifier is current.
  • Check the classification point: good lighting so you can see fat cover and teeth clearly, a safe platform, and enough room to work beside the line.
  • Make sure carcass numbers and producer identification will be visible at your station.

Preparing equipment

  • Roller marks for each age class and the fat codes, clean and complete.
  • Approved food-grade marking ink in the correct colours.
  • Any measuring instrument your abattoir uses for fat, checked and calibrated as the procedure requires.
  • Data sheets or the computer system linked to the correct carcass numbers.

Hygiene and safety

Wear clean protective clothing, a hairnet and gumboots, and the cut-resistant glove or apron your abattoir requires. Wash and sanitise your hands before starting and after touching anything dirty. When you open a carcass mouth to check teeth, use clean hands or the tool provided. Watch out for moving hooks, wet floors and knives used by other workers. Never reach into the moving line, and know where the line stop is.

lessons.title: Performing the classification: age, fat, conformation and damage
lessons.html:
Age class

Age is judged by counting the permanent incisor teeth. Young animals have only milk teeth; as they grow older the permanent incisors come through in pairs.

Age classPermanent incisorsRoller colour
ANone (milk teeth only)Purple
AB1 to 2Green
B3 to 6Brown
CMore than 6Red

A lamb is normally class A. A ewe that has lambed several seasons is usually C. Count carefully: a broken or missing tooth must not lead you to place an old ewe in a younger class.

Fat code

Fat cover is scored from 0 (no fat) to 6 (excessively fat). Look at the fat over the back, loin, ribs and tail area, and use any fat measurement your procedure requires. Buyers usually want codes in the middle of the scale: too lean meat dries out, and too much fat is trimmed off and wasted.

CodeDescription
0No fat
1Very lean
2Lean
3Medium
4Fat
5Overfat
6Excessively fat

Conformation and damage

Conformation describes how well muscled the carcass is, scored from 1 (very flat, poorly muscled) to 5 (very well muscled, rounded). A well-fed Dorper lamb often scores higher than a thin goat.

Damage is scored according to how much bruising or trimming there is, from slight to severe. Note bruising from rough handling in the bakkie, truck or pens. Damage records help farmers and transporters improve how animals are loaded and handled.

Working on the line

  1. Check the carcass number and producer identification.
  2. Count the permanent incisors and decide the age class.
  3. Assess fat cover and give the fat code.
  4. Score conformation and damage.
  5. If you are unsure, look again; if the line is too fast for accurate work, ask your supervisor to slow it.

lessons.title: Completing the classification process
lessons.html:
Marking the carcass

The carcass is marked with the roller for its age class, in the correct colour, showing the fat code. The mark runs along the length of the carcass so it shows on the cuts that reach the butcher counter. A clear, complete mark lets the consumer recognise, for example, that A2 is young lamb with lean fat cover. Use only approved food-grade ink, and replace any roller that is worn or damaged.

Recording results

  • Record age class, fat code, conformation, damage and mass against the right carcass number and producer.
  • Check that the number of carcasses classified equals the number slaughtered for each producer.
  • Note any carcass that could not be classified or was re-assessed, with the reason.
  • Record equipment checks and faults.
  • Hand in or upload the records as your procedure requires and keep copies.

These records are used to pay farmers and to give them feedback. A producer whose lambs often come through with fat code 5 can change the feeding programme or market them earlier. A producer with a lot of bruising damage can look at how animals are handled on the farm and in transport.

End of shift

  1. Clean the roller marks and any measuring instrument as the hygiene plan says, and store them clean and dry.
  2. Report broken or worn equipment and ink running low.
  3. Leave the classification point clean and safe.
  4. Report problems such as missing identification, line speed problems or disputes to your supervisor.

Independence and disputes

Classification must be fair to both seller and buyer. Never change a class to please a producer, buyer or manager. If a producer disputes a class, explain calmly how it was assigned and use the formal dispute process where one exists. Accurate assessment and complete records are your best defence.

Key points

  • Small stock carcasses are classified on age, fat, conformation and damage.
  • Age is judged by counting permanent incisors: A (none), AB (1 to 2), B (3 to 6), C (more than 6).
  • Fat codes run from 0 (no fat) to 6 (excessively fat).
  • Mark carcasses with the correct colour roller and food-grade ink, and record every result against the right carcass.
  • Classification must stay independent and accurate, even under pressure.
